title: The Cherry Orchard | 벚 꽃 동 산 by Simon Stone at Park Avenue Armory #th...
transcript: In one of the most sumptuous productions I've seen in a long time, a wealthy Korean family reunites while their company teeters on the brink of bankruptcy. This play by Simon Stone reimagines The Cherry Orchard, turning Chekhov into a K-drama with English supertitles. It's just as ambitious conceptually as it is physically, set on and around a massive house that's expensive and beautiful, but impractical and ostentatious, much like the people who own it. When the matriarch of the family returns to Korea from the United States with her younger daughter and begins to learn of the family's dire financial circumstances, she's remarkably unfazed. It's not just her, though. The majority of the family lacks concern, completely ignoring the advice of an old friend who eagerly offers them a respectable path forward. Exactly why nobody seems to care is up for debate. Is it arrogance? Is it indifference? Is it learned helplessness? Maybe all of the above. We come to learn that the family has had its share of emotional traumas, so it's no wonder why they're so deeply unwell psychologically. That said, it's their privilege more than anything else that appears to breed their complacency and their refusal to keep up with a rapidly changing world. As you're hit with a mixture of comedy and tragedy, you feel kind of bad for them, but it does get to a point. Aside from the awe-inducing production design, it's a really interesting observational character study and a meditation on class, modernity, and dysfunctional family dynamics. It's a sold out run at Park Avenue Armory through this Saturday, but they have a standby line and a $35 rush, which is how I wound up in the front row. If you can get a ticket, it's worth seeing. With that, another program for my collection.
